       1             SENATOR MARTINS:  Welcome to the

       2      Senate Standing Committee on Local Government's

       3      hearing on fiscally distressed municipalities,

       4      preparing for and preventing municipal bankruptcy in

       5      New York.

       6             This is the third hearing that we will be

       7      holding.

       8             We've held hearings in Syracuse and Buffalo

       9      last week.

      10             We're here in Nassau County this week.

      11             Syracuse first, because Syracuse is one of

      12      those upstate cities and communities that is

      13      teetering on the brink, and, certainly, we heard

      14      about that when we took testimony in Syracuse, and,

      15      certainly, Mayor Miner was very eloquent in her

      16      analysis of their position.

      17             But, certainly, that is replicated throughout

      18      Upstate New York with other cities, Rochester,

      19      Utica, and, certainly, is a wake-up call for all of

      20      us.

      21             We held hearings in Buffalo.

      22             Buffalo, not only Erie County, but the

      23      city of Buffalo themselves have control boards, and

      24      so the focus in Buffalo was on those control boards,

      25      and how effective they've been, and whether or not





 

                                                                   4
       1      there's a model and a best practices to be learned

       2      as a result of both control boards.

       3             And we're now here in Nassau County, another

       4      community that has a control board, now, for

       5      13 years.

       6             And I guess the hope today is, one, let's

       7      talk about some of the pressures that we have on our

       8      local municipalities, and things that we can do,

       9      hopefully, to address those pressures;

      10             But, two, let's talk about that interface

      11      between the control boards and local governments,

      12      and what works, what doesn't work, and  perhaps

      13      better approaches to dealing with issues of

      14      municipal insolvency as we move forward.

      15             As I have said before, I do not believe that

      16      bankruptcy is an option for municipalities.

      17             I think that's a very dangerous precedent in

      18      New York State.

      19             I believe that the model that New York has

      20      used in the past with these control boards has been

      21      more appropriate, but let's learn from our past

      22      practices, and move forward.

      23             We have a wonderful list of experts and

      24      witnesses and municipal experts with us today.

      25             Looking forward to hearing the testimony.

       2             SENATOR MARTINS:  Let's get started.

       3             Our first witness is

       4      Lieutenant Governor Richard Ravitch, who is the

       5      co-chair of the Advisory Board, State Budget Crisis

       6      Task Force.

       7             Governor, good to see you again.

       8             RICHARD RAVITCH:  Nice to see you both.

       9             SENATOR MARTINS:  Thank you.

      10             RICHARD RAVITCH:  Senator, let me begin by

      11      saying how much I respect you for convening these

      12      hearings.

      13             The question of local government distress is

      14      grossly underreported in our media.

      15             There is nothing unique about New York State.

      16             This is a problem that affects practically

      17      every local government throughout the country, some

      18      with greater severity, obviously, than others.

      19             We all know about Detroit.

      20             You will soon be reading about Puerto Rico.

      21             And, you know about cities in California that

      22      have filed under the federal bankruptcy code.

      23             And you will continue to hear a myriad of

      24      stories, states like Illinois and New Jersey, have

      25      no capacity whatsoever to -- financial capacity to





 

                                                                   7
       1      meet the pension obligations that they have incurred

       2      and that are [inaudible].

       3             The State of Colorado has announced that it

       4      would require an expenditure of $15,000 for every

       5      taxpayer in the state to make that system whole.

       6             Respected economists believe that the

       7      public-pension funds of the states of this country

       8      could be underfunded by as much as $4 trillion.

       9             And this problem is getting worse.

      10             And the reason it is getting worse is because

      11      retirement expenditures and health-care expenditures

      12      are growing at a much faster rate than our revenues

      13      at state and local levels.

      14             And, there is -- fiscal stress rolls

      15      downhill.

      16             So, as the federal government addresses and

      17      argues about how to reduce the federal deficit, and

      18      they cut, in some cases, as a result, through the

      19      system of sequestration, in some instances, through

      20      the approval of [inaudible] developmental budgets,

      21      programmatic budgets, which have been cut.

      22             And, if you examine those cuts and

      23      sequestration carefully, you will see a very

      24      significant percentage of that comes out of the

      25      $650 billion or so that constitutes the part of the





 

                                                                   8
       1      federal discretionary budget that is passed through

       2      to states.

       3             And you have to remember that about

       4      30-odd percent of state expenditures come from the

       5      federal government, and almost the same percentage

       6      of local government budgets around the country come

       7      from states.

       8             So, it is intellectually impossible to deal

       9      with the subject without understanding the

      10      interrelationship between the three levels of

      11      government.

      12             And I have to say, one of the reasons why I

      13      commend you so much for having this hearing, is that

      14      the political system, at all three levels, have not

      15      really looked at this in the -- in accurate context.

      16             So there are, I would respectfully suggest,

      17      three fundamental issues:

      18             One is, what can you do about it from -- to

      19      avoid having to face the question, Mr. Chairman,

      20      that you raised about bankruptcy versus control

      21      boards?

      22             How do you get to the point where local

      23      governments have sufficient revenues to meet their

      24      obligations, their -- provide the essential services

      25      that they are charged with providing for their





 

                                                                   9
       1      citizens?

       2             How do you do that in a meaningful way?

       3             Well, I would respectfully suggest that, the

       4      first step, is to require that cities,

       5      school boards, counties, budget in accordance with

       6      generally accepted accounting principles.

       7             The most significant thing that we did, and I

       8      had the honor of being very involved in this in

       9      state government in the '70s, the first thing we

      10      did, when the city of New York was facing the

      11      possibility of filing bankruptcy, was to pass a law

      12      requiring that they budget in accordance with GAAP,

      13      which means, in simple language, that their

      14      recurring revenues have to match their recurring

      15      expenditures; that they couldn't use borrowed money

      16      to balance their operating budgets; that they

      17      couldn't use their capital budgets to balance their

      18      operating budgets; which is what the City of

      19      New York had notoriously done.

      20             And I have to say that, even though the

      21      city of New York has gone through some ups and

      22      downs, not the least of which was 9/11, that there

      23      was never been a budget crisis in New York City, and

      24      I believe that is due largely to the fact that they

      25      have this statutory obligation to budget carefully.





 

                                                                   10
       1             Now, the State has no such obligation.

       2             And, unfortunately, the State has used, over

       3      the last 20-odd years, massive amounts of one-shots

       4      and borrowings to balance its operating budget.

       5             And as a result that of, as more and more

       6      attention is focused on the use of those methods for

       7      balancing budgets and opposing some constraint, and

       8      I hope the elected officials of the state recognize

       9      that that's a no-win strategy, we -- we -- the State

      10      is now facing, and engaging properly in, significant

      11      reductions in the levels of State expenditures, be

      12      it Medicaid, which is the largest consumer of

      13      State dollars, or education, where you, as you well

      14      know better than I have, put a cap on the

      15      [inaudible].

      16             And all of this has a very, very significant

      17      effect on local governments, on school boards, and

      18      on mayors.

      19             And, in an effort to address the

      20      extraordinary level of real-estate taxes that was

      21      growing as a source of revenue, which mayors and

      22      [inaudible] exercised in order to have the cash to

      23      meet their obligations, you legislated a

      24      property-tax cap; a very popular measure, and you

      25      made provision for local governments to override





 

                                                                   11
       1      that cap under certain limited circumstances.

       2             And -- but the fundamental issue here is,

       3      that, as I said, the fiscal stress rolls down hill,

       4      so state and local governments are in for a growing,

       5      growing pressure -- budgetary pressure.

       6             This is not a circumstance that was created

       7      by the economic catastrophe that hit our country in

       8      2008, 2009, and that the problems was structural,

       9      around the country at a state and local level.

      10             And we made promises, as a society, which we

      11      can't -- under our current system of revenue

      12      collection, we can't pay for.  We can't pay for the

      13      obligations we assume.

      14             They were made in good faith.  Serves no

      15      useful purpose going back and criticizing what

      16      people did 20 years ago, or 10 years ago.

      17             They did it.

      18             We were -- we believed we had the ability to

      19      fulfill the obligations that we incurred, but we do

      20      not today.

      21             And, again, this is not unique to New York.

      22             So, I believe that by moving to budgeting on

      23      a GAAP basis, and giving local governments some

      24      period of time, because a lot of them can't get

      25      there overnight, and because banks are perfectly





 

                                                                   12
       1      willing to extend credit and not pay much attention

       2      to how the money is used, a practice that has

       3      contributed significantly to the growing fiscal

       4      pressures that you wisely are attempting to deal

       5      with and understand.

       6             And as we know, in Detroit, the federal

       7      courts are going to decide whether or not the

       8      obligations to pension beneficiaries are superior,

       9      inferior, or equal to the obligations to debt

      10      holders, and that's a very, very important decision.

      11             It will be challenged in courts.

      12             And a discussion of that is already in the

      13      courts.

      14             It's in the courts of Rhode Island, where

      15      they passed a very significant pension-reform

      16      system, and it is being challenged in the courts as

      17      being unconstitutional.

      18             In Illinois, which has language very similar

      19      to the New York State Constitution about the

      20      sanctity of public benefits, there is litigation

      21      arising from the fact that some of the more

      22      distinguished lawyers in Illinois believe that that

      23      constitutional constraint does not prevent the

      24      legislature from amending the benefits for those

      25      employee -- for the balance of the terms of the





 

                                                                   13
       1      current employees, let alone change them for future

       2      employees.

       3             And I could go on and on, but there's

       4      litigation all over the country about the nature of

       5      these obligations, and the power of state

       6      legislatures to modify them.

       7             And -- so having, I hope, proved that we're

       8      not unique in New York, and -- though -- but we are

       9      one of 31 states, only 31 states, that have the

      10      statutory power to file under Chapter 9 of the

      11      federal bankruptcy statutes.

      12             States themselves are not permitted,

      13      constitutionally, to file because of the

      14      11th Amendment to the Constitution.

      15             Local governments can file under the terms of

      16      the bankruptcy statute itself only when authorized

      17      by state law to do so.

      18             And those laws can be limiting, can define

      19      what can happen in bankruptcy, how large a city; how

      20      large a population has to be for a city to be

      21      eligible to file bankruptcy.

      22             And New York has, as a result of amendments

      23      to the federal bankruptcy statute that follow the

      24      near -- the insolvency of New York City in the

      25      mid-'70s, we have a fairly flexible powers, if we





 

                                                                   14
       1      file under the -- if the City files under the

       2      bankruptcy statute.

       3             By the way, that would apply equally to

       4      counties or to school districts or to public-benefit

       5      corporations; they're all in the same category.

       6             So I've tried to outline what I think are the

       7      things that can prevent getting -- local governments

       8      from getting to the point where they are faced with

       9      the necessity of having to do some very, very

      10      drastic things.

      11             Let's talk about if distressed municipalities

      12      get to the point, where as many are in New York, and

      13      others will be over the next couple years,

      14      particularly if sequestration continues at the

      15      federal level, and very much dependent on what you

      16      do with the state budget this year, and this coming

      17      spring, and an election year, and the year after

      18      that.

      19             But on the assumption that the political

      20      constraint, and I don't say this in any way to

      21      denigrate politics, I believe in politics, and the

      22      reason I think bankruptcy is a dreadful option, is

      23      because it's an acknowledgment that democracy can't

      24      solve its problems, and that we're turning it over

      25      to a judge to decide which creditors should get





 

                                                                   15
       1      preference over other creditors.

       2             And in a democracy, if we fail to have people

       3      elected to office make those decisions, either

       4      because they don't have the guts to do it, because

       5      they were very happy making promises and not

       6      worrying about how they were going to be paid for,

       7      is irrelevant.

       8             It's still a dreadful, dreadful result.

       9             I have to tell you, with all respect, that I

      10      don't think control boards are as much of an answer

      11      as some people do, either.

      12             Number one, other than the possible ability,

      13      which the courts upheld, I believe, in

      14      Nassau County, the right of a control board to

      15      freeze wages, I'm not sure that there is any power

      16      conferred to a control board that can't be conferred

      17      to a mayor.

      18             And if, therefore, control boards exist in

      19      many places simply to provide a cover for elected

      20      officials to be able to say, I can't do X, Y, and Z,

      21      or, I must raise taxes, or, I must cut -- close

      22      firehouses, or, I must reduce the number of

      23      police officers, because if I don't, the

      24      control board won't approve my budget; and that

      25      serves a useful function, particularly for people





 

                                                                   16
       1      holding political office that don't have the guts to

       2      make the tough and unpleasant decisions themselves.

       3             But I don't think that's really an answer.

       4             It can buy you some time, but if the

       5      fundamental economics are continuing to go south;

       6      that is, revenues are -- growth is not equaling to

       7      expenditure growth, then a control board isn't going

       8      to solve that problem.

       9             And it is time, therefore, to examine three

      10      things:

      11             I was delighted to hear, Senator, that you

      12      are going to be conducting an investigation of the

      13      tax system in this state.

      14             That is long overdue.

      15             I know the Governor created a commission.

      16             I happen to know the chairman.  He is one the

      17      brightest, most able people.

      18             And I believe they're coming out with a

      19      report in November.

      20             And if you have not talked to them, you

      21      should, off the record, before their report becomes

      22      public, because they've done very exhaustive

      23      research for the last year on that subject.

      24             And, obviously, intending to look at the

      25      question of whether or not we're taxing fairly and





 

                                                                   17
       1      equitably and distributing the burden in a sense of

       2      the way that comports with economic growth, which

       3      I'm sure are the objectives that you have in that

       4      study as well, but one of the inevitable

       5      consequences of such an examination is, also, to

       6      review the potential for revenue growth for the

       7      state and local governments.

       8             And that's very important.

       9             There are mandates created by federal law and

      10      state law that impose burdens on local governments

      11      that were, again, motivated by honorable people.

      12      The reasons were good and sound public policy,

      13      reasons comported with people's sense of fairness

      14      and equity.

      15             We passed a law in New York State called the

      16      "Taylor Law," which prohibited public employees from

      17      going on strike.

      18             I'm very familiar with that, having been the

      19      chairman of the MTA during strikes in metro north,

      20      the Long Island Railroad and the Transit Authority,

      21      and despite the existence of that law.

      22             But the feeling was, in the Legislature, that

      23      in order to address some equities, that instead of

      24      having an expired contract be viewed as no

      25      contractual relationship at all, and have the public





 

                                                                   18
       1      employer being under no obligation to do anything

       2      with its employees, the Legislature passed an

       3      amendment known as the "Triborough Amendment," which

       4      says that the contract shall remain in full force

       5      and effect until no contract is entered into.

       6             So we have this situation in New York City

       7      today, where we have no outstanding

       8      collective-bargaining agreements, and I believe

       9      that's increasingly true around the state.

      10             And it's, ultimately, not a healthy thing for

      11      our society, because, over a long period of time,

      12      unions can't exist without collective-bargaining

      13      agreements, and governments can't budget without

      14      having some rational basis for determining what

      15      their costs are gonna be over the few years.

      16             So I think that issue has to be examined.

      17             I would suggest to you that you look

      18      carefully at the question of whether or not cities

      19      in this state should be relieved from the provisions

      20      in state law that I believe was enacted in 1967,

      21      that says, pension benefits, and terms and

      22      conditions of public pensions, are not bargainable.

      23             Maybe they should be.

      24             Maybe cities should be given the ability to

      25      establish their own pension systems, and not





 

                                                                   19
       1      necessarily be subject to the same requirements that

       2      state employees are subject to.

       3             This is not a suggestion made for the purpose

       4      of diminishing, or necessarily diminishing, the

       5      pension benefits of municipal employees, but it

       6      enables mayors to say, We're not responsible for the

       7      near insolvency we're facing, because our

       8      obligations to pay benefits were set by the

       9      legislature, and not by us.

      10             So maybe you ought to think about giving them

      11      the responsibility in the future to do that.

      12             I think that the obligations which are now

      13      extremely costly -- the OPEB obligations, the

      14      health-care obligations -- they're all contractural,

      15      but because of Triborough, unless there's a mutual

      16      agreement to modify those, they are in full force

      17      and effect.

      18             And we didn't even know what they were until

      19      the Government Accounting Standards Board, a few

      20      years ago, decided to require cities and states to

      21      make them public.

      22             So we now know, New York State has

      23      $65 billion unfunded OPEB liability to its

      24      employees.  The city of New York has an unfunded

      25      OPEB liability of over $100 billion.





 

                                                                   20
       1             And every other city in this state has those

       2      obligations as well.

       3             And third of all, we have to recognize that

       4      the obligations to finance things that cross

       5      municipal and county boundaries, regional issues,

       6      have to be addressed as well.

       7             So, the questions of how the burden gets

       8      shared to pay for the transportation systems in the

       9      New York metropolitan region is a very, very

      10      critical question, because the MTA does not have the

      11      resources to fund another 5-year capital plan, and

      12      that has to be taken into account in evaluating

      13      these systems as well.

      14             So, I don't find control boards -- to

      15      anticipate a question that you may throw my way, I

      16      don't find a control board a -- anywhere near as

      17      violative of the principles of a democratic

      18      political process as I do bankruptcy.

      19             And if it shores-up the backbones -- I'm

      20      mixing my metaphors, forgive me -- stiffens the

      21      backbones of some politicians who don't want to make

      22      tough decisions, that's fine, but it is no solution

      23      for the underlying fundamental disparity between the

      24      growth of revenue and the growth of expenditures in

      25      American society in 2013.

       1             SENATOR MARTINS:  Thank you very much,

       2      Governor.

       3             Senator Marcellino, any questions?

       4             SENATOR MARCELLINO:  Just one.

       5             Governor, if you had a magic wand, and you

       6      could pick one issue or one action that would

       7      probably do the most to solve some of the problems

      10             RICHARD RAVITCH:  Well, I'm not saying this

      11      to be polite.

      12             I would certainly think that what you're

      13      examining about our tax system is critically

      14      important, because the revenue growth is absolutely

      15      important.

      16             Whether that can come by fixing an existing

      17      tax system which is inequitable in many respects, in

      18      which people who should be paying taxes are not

      19      paying taxes, and that is certainly very, very

      20      critically important.

      21             I think, second of all, the disconnect that

      22      exists politically between the State and the cities,

      23      which you are wisely addressing by doing this

      24      hearing, and perhaps by legislative recommendations

      25      when you're finished, that disconnect is even more





 

                                                                   22
       1      severe between the federal and state level.

       2             Let me give you an illustration.

       3             I had occasion recently to meet, it was more

       4      a social circumstance, it wasn't a one-on-one

       5      meeting, where the Chairman of the House Budget

       6      Committee, Paul Ryan, very able man, and I asked

       7      Congressman Ryan, whether or not, when he submitted

       8      a budget that the House of Representatives in

       9      Washington had it approved, did he make any effort

      10      to measure the impact that his budget had on state

      11      and local governments?

      12             And the answer was, no, he did not, because

      13      he didn't think that was part of his responsibility.

      14             His responsibility was to address the federal

      15      budget.

      16             And he asked me why I was so concerned.

      17             And I said:  Well, one of the recommendations

      18      that you made, and so did the Bowles-Simpson Report,

      19      and all the other -- or, many of the other federal

      20      budget proposals to reduce the federal deficit, they

      21      all recommended that the eligibility age of Medicare

      22      be shifted from 65 to 67, thus saving the federal

      23      government hundreds of billions of dollars over

      24      time.

      25             And I said it to the Congressman, and others,





 

                                                                   23
       1      I said:  Are you aware of the fact that states have

       2      contractural obligations, every state, to pay

       3      health-care costs of their employees until they

       4      enter the Medicare program?  So you are not saving

       5      money, you are merely transferring a burden from the

       6      federal tax base to the state and local tax bases.

       7             And there was hardly any recognition of that,

       8      and you've never seen any discussion of that

       9      publicly.

      10             So the second thing I would do, is begin to

      11      make the members of Congress from our state aware

      12      that there is a political price to pay if you don't

      13      examine the issue of your budget actions on state

      14      and local governments.
